blocks.body:
On [[de-rham-cohomology|De Rham cohomology]], integration of top-degree forms gave a map $\int_M:H^n(M)\to\mathbb{R}$ on a compact oriented manifold, and the Mayer–Vietoris sequence computed the groups of spheres, tori and punctured planes. Two things were left open there. On a non-compact manifold the integral of a top-degree form need not exist, and on $\mathbb{R}^n$ every $n$-form is exact, even a bump form with integral $1$, so the integral that detects top-degree classes of compact manifolds detects nothing there. And the Betti numbers of the compact oriented examples were symmetric, $b_k=b_{n-k}$ (for $T^3$ they are $1,3,3,1$), without a reason being given.

Both are explained by forms with compact support. Bott–Tu treat compactly supported cohomology $H^*_c$ as the partner of $H^*$: it has its own Poincaré lemma and its own Mayer–Vietoris sequence, it is covariant for open inclusions where $H^*$ is contravariant, and on an oriented manifold with a finite good cover integration of the wedge product pairs $H^q$ with $H^{n-q}_c$ perfectly. This is Poincaré duality, which Petrov lists among the four major tools of the theory, in the form $H^k(M)\cong H^{n-k}_c(M)^*$.

Papers use duality mostly through one consequence: a closed oriented submanifold $S$ of a compact oriented manifold $M$ has a Poincaré dual class $\eta_S$ with $\int_S\omega=\int_M\omega\wedge\eta_S$. Bhardwaj et al. write charged defects into conservation laws through such delta-forms, and Kreutz–Shen–Vial appeal to Poincaré duality when they relate de Rham–Betti classes to periods. Throughout, the notation, the Mayer–Vietoris sequence with its sign convention, partitions of unity and good covers are those of [[de-rham-cohomology]].

blocks.title: Compact supports and Poincaré duality
blocks.body:
On a non-compact manifold, integration of top forms only makes sense for forms with compact support, and duality statements need them. Let $\Omega^k_c(M)$ be the smooth $k$-forms with compact support; $d$ preserves compact support, and the compactly supported cohomology is
$$H^k_c(M)=\frac{\ker(d:\Omega^k_c\to\Omega^{k+1}_c)}{d(\Omega^{k-1}_c)} .$$
The quotient is by $d$ of compactly supported forms, so a compactly supported form can be exact in $\Omega^*(M)$ but not in $\Omega^*_c(M)$. If $M$ is compact, $H^*_c(M)=H^*(M)$.

Functoriality is different. Pullback of a compactly supported form need not have compact support, so $H_c^*$ is contravariant only for proper maps. On the other hand, for an open subset $j:U\hookrightarrow M$, extension by zero $j_*:\Omega_c^*(U)\to\Omega_c^*(M)$ is a cochain map, so $H^*_c$ is covariant for open inclusions (Bott–Tu, §1–2). For $M=U\cup V$ this gives the compactly supported Mayer–Vietoris sequence: the sequence
$$0\to\Omega_c^*(U\cap V)\to\Omega_c^*(U)\oplus\Omega_c^*(V)\to\Omega_c^*(M)\to0,\qquad\sigma\mapsto(-\sigma,\sigma),\quad(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha+\beta$$
(all maps extension by zero) is exact; surjectivity is $\tau=\rho_U\tau+\rho_V\tau$, and if $\alpha+\beta=0$ then $\alpha=-\beta$ has compact support inside $U\cap V$. Its connecting map $H^k_c(M)\to H^{k+1}_c(U\cap V)$ sends $[\tau]$ to $[d\rho_V\wedge\tau]$: lift $\tau$ to $(\rho_U\tau,\rho_V\tau)$, apply $d$, and note $d\rho_U=-d\rho_V$.

blocks.title: Poincaré lemma for compact supports
blocks.body: $H^k_c(\mathbb{R}^n)=\mathbb{R}$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise, and the isomorphism $H^n_c(\mathbb{R}^n)\to\mathbb{R}$ is $[\omega]\mapsto\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\omega$. Equivalently, a compactly supported $n$-form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is $d$ of a compactly supported $(n-1)$-form if and only if its integral is $0$. (Guillemin–Haine prove the last statement for every connected open subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.)

Write $\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^{n-1}\times\mathbb{R}$ with coordinates $(x,t)$ and $\pi(x,t)=x$. Every compactly supported form is a sum of forms of two types: type I, $f(x,t)\,\varphi$, and type II, $f(x,t)\,\varphi\wedge dt$, with $\varphi=dx_I$ and $f$ compactly supported. Integration along the fibre $\pi_*:\Omega^q_c(\mathbb{R}^n)\to\Omega^{q-1}_c(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})$ kills type I and sends $f\varphi\wedge dt\mapsto\big(\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x,t)\,dt\big)\varphi$. Fix a compactly supported $e(t)$ with $\int e=1$, put $E(t)=\int_{-\infty}^te$, and let $e_*\varphi=\varphi\wedge e(t)\,dt$. Then $\pi_*e_*=\mathrm{id}$, and $\pi_*$, $e_*$ commute with $d$: for type II, $\pi_*d(f\varphi\wedge dt)=\pi_*\big(\sum_j\partial_jf\,dx_j\wedge\varphi\wedge dt\big)=d\big((\int f\,dt)\varphi\big)$, and for type I, $\pi_*d(f\varphi)=(-1)^{|I|}\big(\int\partial_tf\,dt\big)\varphi=0$.

Define $K$ by $K(f\varphi)=0$ and $K(f\varphi\wedge dt)=g\,\varphi$ with $g(x,t)=\int_{-\infty}^tf(x,u)\,du-E(t)\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(x,u)\,du$; $g$ has compact support because for $t$ large both terms equal $\int f$, and for $t$ very negative both vanish. We claim
$$1-e_*\pi_*=(-1)^{q-1}(dK-Kd)\quad\text{on }\Omega^q_c(\mathbb{R}^n).$$
Type I, $\omega=f\varphi$, $q=|I|$: $e_*\pi_*\omega=0$, $K\omega=0$, and the $dt$-part of $d\omega$ is $(-1)^q\partial_tf\,\varphi\wedge dt$, so $Kd\omega=(-1)^q\big(\int_{-\infty}^t\partial_tf-E\int_{\mathbb{R}}\partial_tf\big)\varphi=(-1)^qf\varphi$. Hence $(-1)^{q-1}(dK-Kd)\omega=\omega$. Type II, $\omega=f\varphi\wedge dt$, $q=|I|+1$: $dK\omega=\sum_j\partial_jg\,dx_j\wedge\varphi+(f-eF)\,dt\wedge\varphi$ with $F=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f$, and $Kd\omega=K\big(\sum_j\partial_jf\,dx_j\wedge\varphi\wedge dt\big)=\sum_j\partial_jg\,dx_j\wedge\varphi$. So $dK\omega-Kd\omega=(-1)^{|I|}(f\varphi\wedge dt-F\varphi\wedge e\,dt)=(-1)^{q-1}(\omega-e_*\pi_*\omega)$.

So $e_*\pi_*$ is homotopic to the identity, $\pi_*e_*=\mathrm{id}$, and $\pi_*:H^q_c(\mathbb{R}^n)\to H^{q-1}_c(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})$ is an isomorphism. By induction, $H^q_c(\mathbb{R}^n)\cong H^{q-n}_c(\mathbb{R}^0)$, which is $\mathbb{R}$ for $q=n$ and $0$ otherwise. Iterating $\pi_*$ in degree $n$ is integration over all variables, which identifies the isomorphism with $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}$.

blocks.title: Poincaré duality
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be an oriented $n$-manifold with a finite good cover. The pairing
$$H^q(M)\times H^{n-q}_c(M)\to\mathbb{R},\qquad([\omega],[\tau])\mapsto\int_M\omega\wedge\tau,$$
is well defined and nondegenerate, so $H^q(M)\cong\big(H^{n-q}_c(M)\big)^*$ and, all spaces being finite dimensional, $H^{n-q}_c(M)\cong H^q(M)^*$. If $M$ is compact, $H^q(M)\cong H^{n-q}(M)^*$, so $b_q=b_{n-q}$; if $M$ is moreover connected, $\int_M:H^n(M)\to\mathbb{R}$ is an isomorphism.

Well defined: $\omega\wedge\tau$ has compact support, and changing $\omega$ by $d\eta$ or $\tau$ by $d\sigma$ ($\sigma$ compactly supported) changes the integrand by $d(\eta\wedge\tau)$ or $\pm d(\omega\wedge\sigma)$, which integrate to $0$ by Stokes. Write $PD_M:H^q(M)\to H^{n-q}_c(M)^*$ for the induced map.

Base case: $M\cong\mathbb{R}^n$. Both sides vanish unless $q=0$; for $q=0$, $PD(1)([\tau])=\int\tau$, which is an isomorphism $H^0=\mathbb{R}\to H^n_c(\mathbb{R}^n)^*$ by the compact Poincaré lemma.

Comparison of the two Mayer–Vietoris sequences. For $M=U\cup V$, place the Mayer–Vietoris sequence of $H^*$ above the dual of the compactly supported one (dualising an exact sequence of vector spaces keeps it exact), with the maps $PD$ as vertical arrows:
$$\begin{array}{ccccccc}H^q(M)&\to&H^q(U)\oplus H^q(V)&\to&H^q(U\cap V)&\xrightarrow{\delta}&H^{q+1}(M)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow\\ H^{n-q}_c(M)^*&\to&H^{n-q}_c(U)^*\oplus H^{n-q}_c(V)^*&\to&H^{n-q}_c(U\cap V)^*&\xrightarrow{d_*^{\,*}}&H^{n-q-1}_c(M)^*\end{array}$$
The first two squares commute: $\int_M\omega\wedge j_*\alpha=\int_U\omega|_U\wedge\alpha$, and similarly with the signs $(b-a)$ against $(-\sigma,\sigma)$. For the third, take $\omega$ closed on $U\cap V$ and $\tau\in\Omega^{n-q-1}_c(M)$ closed. The form representing $\delta\omega$ is $-d\rho_V\wedge\omega$ (supported in $U\cap V$), and $d_*\tau=d\rho_V\wedge\tau$. So
$$\int_M\delta\omega\wedge\tau=-\int d\rho_V\wedge\omega\wedge\tau,\qquad\int_{U\cap V}\omega\wedge d_*\tau=(-1)^q\int d\rho_V\wedge\omega\wedge\tau,$$
and the square commutes up to the sign $(-1)^{q+1}$. Changing the sign of some vertical maps makes every square commute without affecting which of them are isomorphisms.

Five lemma. In a commutative diagram of vector spaces with exact rows $A_1\to A_2\to A_3\to A_4\to A_5$ over $B_1\to\cdots\to B_5$, if the vertical maps at positions $1,2,4,5$ are isomorphisms, so is the one at position $3$. (Injectivity: if $a_3\mapsto0$, its image in $A_4$ maps to $0$ in $B_4$, so is $0$; then $a_3$ comes from $a_2$, whose image $b_2$ maps to $0$ in $B_3$, so $b_2$ is the image of some $b_1$, which is the image of some $a_1$; then $a_2$ minus the image of $a_1$ maps to $0$ in $B_2$, hence is $0$, so $a_2$ comes from $A_1$ and $a_3=0$. Surjectivity is the dual chase.)

Induction. Suppose $PD$ is an isomorphism, in all degrees, for every oriented manifold with a good cover of at most $p$ sets, and let $M$ have a good cover $U_1,\dots,U_{p+1}$. With $U=U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_p$ and $V=U_{p+1}$, the manifolds $U$, $V$, $U\cap V$ have good covers of at most $p$ sets. In the ladder around $H^q(M)$, namely $H^{q-1}(U)\oplus H^{q-1}(V)\to H^{q-1}(U\cap V)\to H^q(M)\to H^q(U)\oplus H^q(V)\to H^q(U\cap V)$, the four outer vertical maps are isomorphisms, so $PD_M$ is one. The statements for compact and connected $M$ follow from $H^*_c=H^*$, finite dimensionality and $H^0(M)=\mathbb{R}$, where $PD(1)=\int_M$.

blocks.title: Poincaré dual of a submanifold
blocks.body:
Let $M$ be a compact oriented $n$-manifold and $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ a closed oriented $k$-dimensional submanifold. The functional $[\omega]\mapsto\int_Si^*\omega$ on $H^k(M)$ is linear, so by Poincaré duality there is a unique class $\eta_S\in H^{n-k}(M)$ with
$$\int_Si^*\omega=\int_M\omega\wedge\eta_S\qquad\text{for all closed }\omega\in\Omega^k(M).$$
This is the Poincaré dual of $S$ (Bott–Tu, §5). It can be represented by a closed form supported in any given tubular neighbourhood of $S$, a bump form concentrated near $S$; physicists call such representatives delta-forms, and Bhardwaj et al. write $\delta^{d-p}(M_p)$ for the form dual to a $p$-dimensional submanifold $M_p$ of spacetime. The order $\omega\wedge\eta_S$ is a convention; using $\eta_S\wedge\omega$ changes $\eta_S$ by $(-1)^{k(n-k)}$.

In words: integrating over $S$ is the same as wedging with $\eta_S$ and integrating over all of $M$.

blocks.title: Poincaré duals of circles on the torus
blocks.body: On $T^2$ with orientation $d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2$, let $S=\{\theta_1=0\}$ (oriented by $\theta_2$) and $T=\{\theta_2=0\}$ (oriented by $\theta_1$). Find $\eta_S$ and $\eta_T$ and compute $\int_{T^2}\eta_S\wedge\eta_T$ and $\int_T\eta_S$.
blocks.solution:
By the Künneth computation on [[de-rham-cohomology|De Rham cohomology]], $H^1(T^2)$ has basis $[d\theta_1],[d\theta_2]$, so test against $\omega=a\,d\theta_1+b\,d\theta_2$. On $S$, $i^*\omega=b\,d\theta_2$, so $\int_S\omega=2\pi b$. Try $\eta_S=c\,d\theta_1$: then $\omega\wedge\eta_S=bc\,d\theta_2\wedge d\theta_1=-bc\,d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2$, with integral $-4\pi^2bc$. So $c=-\frac1{2\pi}$ and $\eta_S=-\frac1{2\pi}[d\theta_1]$. The bump representative is $-\rho(\theta_1)\,d\theta_1$ with $\int\rho=1$ and $\rho$ supported near $\theta_1=0$, which is cohomologous to it (both have period $0$ over $S$ and $-1$ over $T$, so they agree because [[de-rham-cohomology|periods determine classes]]). Similarly $\int_T\omega=2\pi a$, and $\eta_T=c'\,d\theta_2$ gives $\int a c'\,d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2=4\pi^2ac'$, so $\eta_T=\frac1{2\pi}[d\theta_2]$.

Then $\int_{T^2}\eta_S\wedge\eta_T=-\frac1{4\pi^2}\cdot4\pi^2=-1$, and directly $\int_T\eta_S=\int_0^{2\pi}-\frac1{2\pi}\,d\theta_1=-1$, as the defining property with $\omega=\eta_S$ predicts. The value $\pm1$ is the signed count of the single intersection point of $S$ and $T$; at that point the tangent vectors of $S$ then $T$, namely $(\partial_{\theta_2},\partial_{\theta_1})$, form a negatively oriented basis, which accounts for the sign. Guillemin–Haine obtain intersection numbers of submanifolds as a consequence of Poincaré duality, through Thom classes (§5.5).

items.label: Nondegenerate integration pairing
items.body: Bott–Tu and Guillemin–Haine state duality as the nondegeneracy of $\int_M\omega\wedge\tau$ between $H^q$ and $H^{n-q}_c$; Bott–Tu prove it by the Mayer–Vietoris ladder and the five lemma, starting from the two Poincaré lemmas on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

items.label: An isomorphism with a dual
items.body: Petrov states it as $H^k(M)\cong H^{n-k}_c(M)^*$ for connected oriented $M$, and warns that the reverse statement $H^k_c\cong(H^{n-k})^*$ is not always true: dualising turns a direct sum into a direct product, but the dual of a direct product is not a direct sum, so the argument cannot be run backwards when the spaces are infinite dimensional.

items.label: Submanifolds as forms
items.body: Every closed oriented submanifold $S$ defines a class $\eta_S$ with $\int_S=\int_M(\,\cdot\,)\wedge\eta_S$. Intersections of submanifolds become wedge products of their duals, and in field theory a charged defect on $M_p$ enters the conservation law through its delta-form, $dj=q\,\delta(M_p)$.

items.label: Integration to a point
items.body: Notman–Sanabani phrase top-degree integration as a linear map $\int_M:H^\bullet(M)\to H^\bullet(\mathrm{pt})$, nonzero only in degree $n$. In this form it generalises to the equivariant setting, where it lands in the equivariant cohomology of a point, and that is the language of their localisation theorems.

blocks.body:
- On a non-compact manifold, Poincaré duality pairs $H^q$ with compactly supported $H^{n-q}_c$, not with $H^{n-q}$. For $\mathbb{R}^n$: $H^0=\mathbb{R}$ while $H^n=0$; the partner of $H^0$ is $H^n_c=\mathbb{R}$.
- $H^*_c$ is not a homotopy invariant: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is contractible but $H^n_c(\mathbb{R}^n)=\mathbb{R}\ne H^n_c(\mathrm{pt})$ for $n\ge1$. It is invariant under proper homotopies, and covariant (not contravariant) for open inclusions.
- A compactly supported form can be exact without being compactly exact: a bump $n$-form on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with integral $1$ is $d$ of some $(n-1)$-form, but of no compactly supported one.
- Orientation is needed. Without it $\int_M$ is not defined, and for the non-orientable compact Klein bottle $H^2=0$ (see the Klein bottle example on [[de-rham-cohomology|De Rham cohomology]]), so $H^0\not\cong(H^2)^*$.
- Sign and order conventions for $\eta_S$ ($\omega\wedge\eta_S$ versus $\eta_S\wedge\omega$, orientation of the normal bundle) differ between sources; check one example such as the torus above before comparing formulas.

blocks.title: Conventions for compact supports and Poincaré duals
blocks.body: Collected from the statements above; the signs matter when a paper writes an explicit dual form or a commuting ladder.

rows.text: $H^k_c(M)$ for compactly supported cohomology. Compactly supported Mayer–Vietoris with $\sigma\mapsto(-\sigma,\sigma)$ and $(\alpha,\beta)\mapsto\alpha+\beta$, connecting map $[\tau]\mapsto[d\rho_V\wedge\tau]$. Against the ordinary sequence with difference map $(\omega,\tau)\mapsto\tau-\omega$, the square of connecting maps in the duality ladder commutes up to $(-1)^{q+1}$.

$\int_Si^*\omega=\int_M\omega\wedge\eta_S$ (Bott–Tu, §5, and this page); writing $\eta_S\wedge\omega$ instead changes $\eta_S$ by $(-1)^{k(n-k)}$. With this order, on $T^2$ oriented by $d\theta_1\wedge d\theta_2$, the circle $\{\theta_1=0\}$ oriented by $\theta_2$ has dual $-[d\theta_1]/2\pi$.
$\delta^{d-p}(M_p)$, or $\delta(M_p)$, for the delta-form Poincaré dual to a $p$-dimensional submanifold $M_p$ of $d$-dimensional spacetime.

blocks.body:
1. Compute $H^*_c(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\})$ and $H^*_c$ of the open Möbius band, and compare with $H^*$ of these spaces.
2. Show that $H^1_c(\mathbb{R})\cong\mathbb{R}$ by integration, directly from the definition (a compactly supported $f\,dx$ is $dg$ with $g$ compactly supported iff $\int f=0$).
3. Use Poincaré duality to show that every compact connected orientable $3$-manifold has $\chi=0$.
4. On $S^2\times S^2$ let $A=S^2\times\{p\}$ and $B=\{p\}\times S^2$. Express $\eta_A,\eta_B$ in terms of the normalised area forms of the two factors and compute $\int\eta_A\wedge\eta_B$, $\int\eta_A\wedge\eta_A$.
5. Let $M$ be compact oriented and $f:M\to M$ smooth. Show that $\int_M f^*\mu$ for a normalised volume form $\mu$ is a well-defined number depending only on the homotopy class of $f$ (this is the degree of $f$).

This page rests on [[de-rham-cohomology]]: the Mayer–Vietoris sequence and its connecting map, good covers, the Poincaré lemma, and integration with Stokes' theorem. Poincaré duality for singular cohomology belongs to [[cohomology]]; over $\mathbb{R}$ de Rham's theorem identifies the two settings. Bott–Tu continue with the Thom isomorphism and the Thom class of an oriented vector bundle (their §6), through which Guillemin–Haine (§5.5) obtain intersection numbers of submanifolds; Euler and Chern classes are on [[curvature-forms]], with [[vector-bundles]]. Delta-forms also appear in the physics dictionary on [[de-rham-cohomology]], which continues in [[yang-mills]]. For finite elements, Guzmán–Hirani–Liu–Potu give a discrete counterpart of compactly supported potentials on star-shaped domains: they modify their discrete Poincaré operator into a Bogovskiĭ operator, which satisfies the same homotopy identity but sends forms with homogeneous boundary conditions (forms that extend by zero outside the domain) to potentials with the same property; in top degree such forms have integral zero, the condition of the compact Poincaré lemma.
